disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation) is characterized by developmentally inappropriate levels of motor activity, restlessness, talkativeness, and impulsive behaviors, with comparatively fewer or less impairing inattentive symptoms. Individuals often display difficulty remaining seated, acting without considering consequences, interrupting others, and feeling internally driven to be constantly active, leading to problems in school, work, or social settings. Onset is typically in childhood, but functional impairment may become more prominent or clinically recognized only when environmental demands increase, such as in higher education or complex jobs. It is differentiated from anxiety, mood, and substance-related disorders by the pervasive, long-standing pattern of hyperactive-impulsive behavior across settings and by the absence of episodic mood changes or primary substance effects as the central cause.

narrative.personality: Maritza is a free-spirited, curious, and hardworking young woman who thrives on movement, novelty, and hands-on problem-solving out on the road.
narrative.stressor: Maritza’s symptoms became clinically significant after she transitioned from casual local delivery work during high school to full-time regional trucking with tighter schedules and longer solo drives. The expectation to sit still for hours, follow strict safety protocols, and manage paperwork at distribution centers clashed sharply with her natural drive to keep moving, chatting, and constantly doing something. Over about eight months, dispatchers and supervisors began documenting concerns about her restlessness at loading docks, difficulty staying put during mandatory safety briefings, and impulsive behavior at customer sites, which led to formal warnings and near loss of a key contract. When her company required her to meet with an occupational health provider after a complaint from a warehouse manager about her inability to remain in designated areas, she agreed to a psychiatric referral, worried that what she had always seen as just being “high-energy” was now putting her job and long-term dream of owning a logistics firm at risk.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I can’t ever just sit still on the job, like I’m always on the move even when I’m supposed to be waiting.”

narrative.personality: Armando is a disciplined, methodical, and solitary engineer who values structure, precision, and quiet craftsmanship in both his work and hobbies.
narrative.stressor: Armando’s longstanding tendency to stay busy and talk through his ideas became problematic after a major reorganization at his plant placed him in a semi-remote principal engineer track, with more time spent in quiet design reviews, remote meetings, and mentoring sessions instead of hands-on shop work. The shift demanded that he sit through long, silent conference calls, focus on others’ presentations, and then relax during off-hours—expectations that contrasted with his habit of constantly tinkering, pacing, and narrating his thought process while working on models or woodworking projects. Over the following eight months, colleagues began commenting on his difficulty keeping meetings calm and structured, and his attempts to "help" by constantly moving around the lab or talking over quieter team members led to feedback from management that his style was disruptive in the new collaborative environment. Concerned that this long-standing restlessness, which he had always channeled into productive activity, was now jeopardizing his prospects for a senior leadership role, he sought psychiatric evaluation at the suggestion of his primary care physician after a performance review highlighted these behavioral patterns.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Even when I’m supposed to be relaxing or just listening quietly, I find myself needing to move around or talk through everything I’m doing.”

narrative.personality: Samuel is a meticulous, tech-obsessed loner who channels intense focus into his projects and collections, often prioritizing personal technical pursuits over social life.
narrative.stressor: Samuel’s difficulties came into focus when his company shifted from mostly field-based installation work to a mixed role that required longer stretches of quiet lab testing, documentation, and collaborative design sessions for 5G deployments. Accustomed to being on-site, moving between towers, and constantly hands-on with equipment, he struggled with the expectation to sit still in shared workspaces, concentrate silently while others worked nearby, and then unwind at home without turning every evening into a frenetic series of projects. Over about eight months, coworkers in the lab complained that his constant movement, side conversations, and tendency to turn routine tasks into noisy, multitasked mini-projects were distracting, and a supervisor noted that his inability to stay settled during planning meetings was starting to affect project timelines. When a long-time ham radio friend commented that he seemed “wired all the time” and his manager suggested an evaluation after multiple HR notes about his disruptive energy in quiet environments, Samuel agreed to see a psychiatrist to understand why his usual way of operating was suddenly clashing with the demands of his evolving role.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Whenever I’m supposed to just work quietly or relax, I end up fussing with something or moving around instead of staying calm.”
